# R6 Digest — David Intro 16–18 (10112–11917)

Source slice: `.cache/tsumura-1sam-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R6_david_16-18_10112-11917.txt`  
Corresponding raw lines: **10112–11917** (pages ~412–489 of Tsumura NICOT 1 Samuel).  
Scope: IV. “Story of Saul and David” overview; David anointing (16); Goliath (17); Jonathan covenant / Saul enmity (18).

All claims below are **Tsumura-attributed** and grounded only in this range.

---

### C-R6-01
**Claim:** Tsumura frames 1 Sam 16:1–31:13 as the “Story of Saul and David,” in which God as “Lord of History” providentially guides Saul’s decline and David’s rise; the emphasis is on **internal/spiritual** relationships with God more than political actions.  
**Quote:** “In the rest of 1 Samuel, God, the Lord of History, providentially guides the lives of two persons, Saul and David, the former’s decline and the latter’s rise. However, the emphasis is not so much on their political actions as on their internal conditions, that is, their spiritual relationships with God.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 1–3; p. 412  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-02
**Claim:** Saul is portrayed as “like a man living under a curse,” caught in something larger than himself; David is also “caught up in events he cannot control.” Tsumura rejects simple deterministic readings (Saul mere victim / David mere destined success).  
**Quote:** “Saul is ‘like a man living under a curse.’ … Then, was Saul ‘a victim’ of tragic fate and David destined to be a success? The subsequent courses of these two men’s lives show complexities and avoid any simple deterministic understandings.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 3–6; p. 412  
**Targets:** [[saul]], [[david]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-03
**Claim:** David advances toward kingship by the special favor/grace of the Lord who was with him; the Lord’s presence with David is the secret of success and the **theological leitmotif** of the story of David’s rise.  
**Quote:** “In David’s case ‘everything seems inevitably to go well, and he advances step by step toward the kingship’ by the special favor (i.e., grace) of the Lord who was with him. The Lord’s presence with David was the secret of his success and is the theological leitmotif of the story of David’s rise.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 6–8; p. 412  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[divine-providence]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-04
**Claim:** The story has been compared with the Hittite “Apology of Ḫattušili III” and treated as apologetic defense of David against charges of complicity in Saulide deaths; Tsumura denies that the biblical narrative is strictly an “apology” because an apology is first-person “I,” while this story is third-person.  
**Quote:** “However, strictly speaking, our story is not an ‘apology,’ for an ‘apology’ is written in the first person ‘I,’ while this story is narrated from the third person. The biblical narrator seems to be much more interested in the destinies of the chosen individuals, Saul and David, rather than in David’s ‘rise’ to political power.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 10–14; p. 412  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-05
**Claim:** Whether the Lord was with his anointed matters more to the narrator than political achievement; the theme of God’s presence with David accords with the earlier theme of the ark’s presence among the covenant people (chs. 1–7). The Story begins with God present with David through his Spirit and ends with Saul’s death.  
**Quote:** “To him, whether the Lord was with his anointed is more important than what the king or the king-designate achieved in his life. The theological theme of God’s presence with David in this part of 1 Samuel is in accordance with the earlier theme of the presence of the ark among the covenant people in chs. 1–7.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 14–16; p. 412  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-06
**Claim:** Tsumura gives a structural overview of the entire IV block “Story of Saul and David” (16:1–31:13):  
A. Introduction of David (16:1–23)  
B. David and Goliath: Battle at the Valley of Elah (17:1–54)  
C. Saul, Jonathan, and David (17:55–18:5)  
D. Saul becomes David’s enemy (18:6–30)  
E. Saul’s attempts to kill David (19:1–21:1)  
F. David’s escape from Saul (21:1–26:25) with sub-units (Nob massacre; En-gedi; Abigail; Hachilah)  
G. David in Philistia (27:1–30:31) incl. Witch of Endor (28:3–25)  
H. Death of Saul and Jonathan (31:1–13)  
**Quote:** “It might be useful for the reader to have an overview of the structure of this entire ‘Story of Saul and David’ (16:1–31:13) at this point.” [followed by A–H outline]  
**Locus:** slice ll. 18–36; pp. 412–413  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-07
**Claim:** Against McCarter (who begins “Rise of David” at 16:14 and takes 15:35–16:13 as brace with Saul’s rejection), Tsumura keeps 15:35 with the previous section and treats **16:1** as “a” of the **A/aB Transitional Technique**: A (15:1–35) / a (16:1) B (16:2–13).  
**Quote:** “It is more reasonable to explain 16:1 as a link that recapitulates the preceding episode, thus constituting ‘a’ of the ‘Transitional Technique,’ the A/aB pattern … A (15:1–35)/ a (16:1) B (16:2–13).”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 45–50; p. 413  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-08
**Claim:** Verses 16:1–13 as a whole also function as “a” linking the whole “Story of Saul” to the “Story of Saul and David”: A (9:1–15:35) / a (16:1–13) B (16:14–31:13). The anointing episode refers back to Saul’s election/rejection and God’s promise to choose a replacement; focus shifts gradually from Saul toward David.

### C-R6-09
**Claim:** Ch. 16 divides into two selections of David: vv. 1–13 God chooses David; vv. 13–23 Saul chooses David; the second choice results from the first (reader knows; Saul will take time to admit it: 18:8; 24:20).  
**Quote:** “Chapter 16 is divided into two sections. In the first section, vv. 1–13, God chooses David; in the second, vv. 13–23, it is Saul who chooses David. The reader knows that the second choice was the result of the first.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 60–62; p. 414  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-10
**Claim:** 16:1—Lord rebukes Samuel’s ongoing grief over Saul with perfect “I have already rejected him” vs. Samuel’s continuous grieving; “I myself” sharply contrasts “you” and “I.” Horn of oil (vs. flask in 10:1); Jesse the Bethlehemite debuts; “I have found … a king for me.”  
**Quote:** “The use of the perfect have already rejected (me’astîw) here is in sharp contrast with the participle which describes Samuel’s ongoing state of ‘grieving’; God’s thoughts and ways are certainly not those of man … The Lord has already made up his mind to choose another man suitable for his work.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 100–112; pp. 414–415  
**Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R6-11
**Claim:** Klein’s claim that David is anointed “king” whereas Saul was anointed “prince” is **not** made by the text; David is elsewhere nāgîd; he is not officially anointed king until 2 Sam 2:4 and 5:3; “to anoint David as king” never appears in ch. 16. While Saul was chosen for the people’s desire, the Lord chooses this king on his own (“for me”).  
**Quote:** “Klein says that ‘David is to be anointed king whereas Saul had been anointed prince (cf. 9:16).’ However, the text does not make this point. … David is not officially anointed as king until 2 Sam. 2:4 and 5:3; in fact, the expression ‘to anoint David as king’ never appears in the present chapter … While Saul was chosen because of the people’s desire for a king (8:5; 10:24), the Lord chooses this king on his own; so I have found … for me.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 112–113; p. 415  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-12
**Claim:** Philology of “heifer”: ‘eglat bāqār = “young female of the cattle,” grammatical adj. construct + genitive (like na‘ar hakkōhēn); acceptable as peace offering (Lev 3:1). bazzābaḥ = “at the feast,” with Ugar. dbḥ “sacrifice, feast.”  
**Quote:** “A heifer is literally ‘the young female (one) of the cattle’ (‘eglat bāqār …), which is grammatically an <adj. construct> + <genitive> like na‘ar hakkōhēn … The Hebrew phrase bazzābaḥ, which literally means ‘in the sacrifice,’ signifies ‘at the time of the feast’ …”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 115–122; pp. 415–416  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

According to Mettinger, ‘Eliab is something of a “new Saul,” so that in his rejection Saul is denounced in effigy.’”

### C-R6-15
**Claim:** Core theological/philological claim of 16:7: “my way of seeing is not like man’s”; man judges **by the eyes** (la‘ênayim = by what he sees; lamed of specification), Lord judges **by the heart** (yir’eh lallēbāb = “sees to the heart” = man’s internal condition). Semantic twist: eyes belong to the judging man; heart belongs to the one judged, not the Lord.  
**Quote:** “But, semantically c//c′ are twisted in terms of their possessors: the ‘eyes’ are the eyes of the man who is judging, while the ‘heart’ is the heart of the one being judged, not of the Lord. The expression judges by the heart (yir’eh lallēbāb) literally means ‘sees to the heart’; the Lord judges man according to the man’s heart, that is, his internal condition.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 217–226; pp. 419–420  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-16
**Claim:** On Jesse’s seven/eight sons: Samuel texts imply David is eighth (also 17:12); 1 Chr 2:15 has seventh. Tsumura rejects “careless” seven-count; argues David is actually seventh **and** climactically “eighth,” via 7//8 epic number parallelism (Ugaritic KTU parallels; Mic 5:5; Rev 17:11). Chronicle lists actual number; Samuel uses epic climax that youngest eclipsed “seven” older brothers.  
**Quote:** “However, one might argue that David was actually the seventh son (so 1 Chr. 2:15) as well as climactically the ‘eighth,’ just as in Mic. 5:5 … Therefore, the Samuel passages, here and 17:12, probably adopt the practice of epic writing, explaining the number of Jesse’s sons as climactically ‘eight’ even though the actual number was seven …”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 234–238; pp. 420–421  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-17
**Claim:** Choice of the youngest is an OT motif (Jacob/Esau; Ephraim/Manasseh); Ugaritic parallel of making youngest firstborn (KTU 1.15:III:16). Shepherding the flock: too much to read future kingship into this (contra Klein); 2 Sam 7:8 rather contrasts shepherd and king roles.  
**Quote:** “Even though kings were often described as shepherds both in Israel and in the ancient Near East, it is probably too much to read into the text a reference to David’s future role as a king, as Klein does. 2 Sam. 7:8 seems rather to contrast David’s roles as shepherd and king.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 246–248; pp. 421–422  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-19
**Claim:** Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David from that day onwards (same formula as Saul 10:6; 11:6). Contrast of “spasmodical” spirit on Saul vs “permanent” on David has been over-emphasized; by v. 14 the spirit had not yet left Saul that day. Name **David** debuts climactically with the onrush of the spirit; first extra-biblical attestation: 9th-c. Aramaic Tel Dan inscription; most promising etymology: Hebrew dôd “beloved.”  
**Quote:** “Just as the spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul ‘on that day’ (10:9) … so it rushed upon David from that day onwards. The contrast has been too much emphasized between the ‘spasmodical’ aspect of the spirit upon Saul and the ‘permanent’ endowment of the spirit upon David … As the following verse (v. 14) notes, the spirit of the Lord had not yet left Saul by that day. … Here the name David (dāwīd) makes its debut in the Bible.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 276–284; pp. 423–424  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-22
**Claim:** Major philological/theological thesis (Excursus): “an evil spirit from the Lord” is inadequate; rûaḥ-rā‘āh is a **construct chain** “a spirit of evilness (or disaster),” not “evil spirit” with adjective—because rā‘āh cannot be adj. in rûaḥ hārā‘āh (16:23) and rûaḥ YHWH rā‘āh (19:9). Parallel to ’anšê rā‘āh “men of evil” (not “evil men”); objective genitive/genitive of effect. Block: “bad” because effects are negative/destructive. Not dualistic pagan “evil spirit vs good spirit”; under God’s sovereignty; plays part in divine plan (McCarter).  
**Quote:** “However, this is not so much a theological as a linguistic problem. The translation ‘an evil spirit from the Lord’ is not adequate for the Hebrew original. We would like to suggest that the phrase rûaḥ-rā‘āh, which is usually translated as ‘an evil spirit,’ should be taken as a construct chain, ‘a spirit of evilness (or disaster),’ since rā‘āh cannot be an adjective in rûaḥ hārā‘āh (16:23) and rûaḥ YHWH rā‘āh (19:9).”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 335–346; pp. 426–428  
**Targets:** [[saul]], [[divine-providence]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

However, there is no direct biblical evidence of deification of instruments in Israel. … The fact remains, however, that music has a therapeutic power.”

### C-R6-24
**Claim:** Officer’s résumé of David (16:18): skillful lyre; gibbôr ḥayil + ’îš milḥāmāh—Tsumura argues these may refer to **Jesse/family background** (ruling class, trained fighter) rather than David’s personal war experience, avoiding contradiction with Saul’s “you are young” in 17:33. “Prudent in speech,” handsome; climax: **“for the Lord is with him!”**—explains all prior qualifications; becomes leitmotiv of David–Saul stories.

### C-R6-25
**Claim:** Philology of ḥămôr leḥem (16:20): lit. “an ass of bread”—not KJV “ass laden with bread,” not LXX/McCarter omer (too small for royal gift), not NEB emended homer. Best: ḥămôr is a **calque** (loan translation) of Akkadian imēru “ass”-measure (~80–160 liters). nō(’)d may be liquid unit/skin-bottle. List-expression “kid of she-goats—one.”  
**Quote:** “The first item in the list of gifts is ḥămôr leḥem, literally, ‘an ass of bread.’ … The best solution is to recognize that the term ḥămôr is a calque (loan translation) of the Akkadian imēru ‘ass’-measure of about 80–160 liters.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 430–436; p. 431  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-29
**Claim:** MT vs LXX on ch. 17: LXX lacks ~46% of MT (27/58 verses: 17:12–31, 41, 48b, 50, 55–58). Positions: Wellhausen/Barthélemy/Gooding/Rofé/van der Kooij—LXX abridgment of longer Hebrew like MT; McCarter/Caird/Stoebe/Hertzberg/Klein—MT expansion of shorter original (LXXB); Tov/Lust—two Hebrew versions, MT combined them leaving contradictions. Tsumura: differences overemphasized; many only superficial; prioritizes “straight and strict” plain-sense reading before accepting inconsistencies.  
**Quote:** “However, these scholars seem to overemphasize the difference of editions, traditions, perspectives, or even theologies between the two ‘versions.’ It is arguable that many such differences are only superficial. … Straight and strict exegetical efforts to read and seek the plain meaning of the text are needed foremost before accepting ‘inconsistencies’ or ‘discrepancies’ in an ancient narrative.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 470–483; pp. 434–436  
**Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-33
**Claim:** Goliath height: MT six cubits and a span (~9 ft 9 in / ~3 m). McCarter thinks six cubits exaggeration; Tsumura: lowering of number in some versions is deliberate; huge weapons (cuirass 126 lbs) make six cubits better sense. Ford: gigantism from pituitary dysfunction. Name Goliath: non-Semitic/Anatolian proposals; better compare Ugaritic PN glyt/n; appears only twice by name in ch. 17 (vv. 4, 23), else “the Philistine” 27× in 17:1–18:5. Rejects identifying 17 with Elhanan’s Goliath (2 Sam 21:19)—too many differences.  
**Quote:** “McCarter thinks that six cubits is an exaggeration. However, the lowering of the number in some versions seems to be deliberate; when one considers the huge size of his weapons (note that his cuirass weighed 126 pounds; see v. 5), six cubits makes better sense. … six cubits and a half … is about 9 feet 9 inches, about 3 meters.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 642–648; pp. 440–441  
**Targets:** [[philistines]], [[david]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-34
**Claim:** Goliath’s weapons detailed to impress human impossibility of prevailing; AXB insertion slows discourse (v.4 came out … vv.5–7 weapons … v.8 stood). Champion = man who steps out between battle lines (de Vaux); Hittite parallel. Scale-armor, bronze helmet, greaves, kîdôn as scimitar (Molin/McCarter), spear like weaver’s beam (mass preferred over heddle-rod theory), iron spear-point 600 shekels (~15 lbs)—fitting early iron age. Shield-bearer with large standing shield ṣinnāh.  
**Quote:** “The champion Goliath and his weapons are described here in detail to impress upon the audience the human impossibility of anyone’s prevailing against him. … Goliath’s entire body was well shielded except his face. Therefore, no ordinary sword-wielding warrior could threaten him. However, with his huge and heavy armor, Goliath’s movement was naturally slow (cf. David’s quick movements in vv. 48–51).”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 604–688; pp. 439–444  
**Targets:** [[philistines]], [[david]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R6-35
**Claim:** Goliath’s challenge (*ḥrp key word: contempt/defiance) offers slave-terms if either side wins—taunt not negotiation, so later non-fulfillment (vv. 52–54) not a legal breach. Israelites “greatly dismayed and frightened”; Philistines highly civilized Aegean-origin, not uncultivated.  
**Quote:** “As this was a taunt speech, not a negotiation, it is not surprising that the promise was not kept. So, it is pointless to talk about the Philistines’ not keeping this agreement in vv. 52–54. … Far from being ‘uncultivated’ uncircumsized people, as the recent archaeological excavations have disclosed, they were highly civilized people, having originated in the Aegean culture.”
